prompt:
TASK: READ ONE INSTRUMENT ENTRY AND ANSWER THREE QUESTIONS

Below is one entry from the specification of a web measurement instrument. The instrument checks
public websites of U.S. federal statistical agencies and reports, per agency, whether each check
passed or failed. The entry states the check's question, the behavior a ready publisher is
expected to show (with verbatim quotes from the sources it cites), the test the instrument runs,
and what a pass and a fail claim.

Terms the project defines once for every entry (they are not undefined): SI client (SI system): a system that finds, reads and uses data on its own, such as an answer engine, an agent or a retrieval pipeline; the project's term for what is elsewhere called an AI system; data page: an agency's own web page for one data product, the page the harness measures (also 'product page' in rule code); harness: this project's scanner: an identified, robots-compliant HTTP client that fetches the pages and records what it met; cycle of record: the scan whose results the published grid is built from (here scan_2026-10-07_composite_d); recorded location: an address for an agency's API, terms, changelog or inventory that the harness was given, read from the agency's own pages or seeded from a named source; error / not measured: the harness could not observe: an access denial, its own robots compliance, an absence it could not confirm, or a server or network error; never a fail

Answer from the entry alone. For question 1, the QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES are the only evidence of
what the sources say; do not use what you know of them from elsewhere.

1. Does the EXPECTED BEHAVIOR come from the cited sources and not from the writer? Answer "yes"
   if every requirement the expected-behavior text attributes to a source is supported by a
   quoted passage, and any part no source defines is said plainly to be undefined or the
   project's own. Answer "no" if it states as a source's requirement something the passages do
   not contain; name it.
2. Could a reader who knows the agency misread a FAIL on this check as a claim the test did not
   make? Answer "yes" if the CLAIMS leave such a misreading open (name it), "no" if they close it.
3. Is any term in the entry undefined for a technically literate reader new to this project?
   Answer "yes" and list the terms, or "no".

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
{"q1": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q2": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q3": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "terms": ["..."], "why": "..."}}

ENTRY
CHECK: A10 (RULE-A10-v3)

QUESTION:
Does the agency's interactive data tool answer a machine client honestly: real content at a deep link, and a real error for a route that does not exist? An SI client that receives HTTP 200 with an error page, or an empty shell that needs a browser to fill, records a page that is not there or reads nothing.
Established by: w3c-dwbp-2017 (Best Practice 23 (programmatic access returns expected responses)); usafacts-ai-ready-data-guide (§4 Open: ensure text documentation is accessible to both humans and AI/web crawlers)

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR:
A route that does not exist answers 404 (or 410): "the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource" (RFC 9110 §15.5.5). A 200 whose content says the page is an error is a soft 404, which Google treats as an error, not a page. A deep link to the product is served (not 4xx/5xx). No cited source requires a data tool's content to be present before JavaScript runs: Google's own crawler renders JavaScript ("Googlebot queues all pages with a 200 HTTP status code for rendering"), and the app-shell model it describes is supported.
Cited sources: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt (§15.5.5 404 Not Found); https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes (200 (success): soft 404 error); https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics (How Google processes JavaScript; app shell model)

QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES (verbatim):
- [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt] "indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource"
- [https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes] "Search Console will show a soft 404 error"
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics] "Googlebot queues all pages with a 200 HTTP status code for rendering"

TEST:
Client: the harness's identified, robots-compliant client; no renderer (params.a10_soft404.renderer: none)
Request: GET the tool's deep link; GET the same tool with the suffix /__ai-readiness-kg-probe-404__
Reads: both statuses; error-shell tokens in the invalid route's body; visible characters in the deep link before JavaScript
Decision rule:
- fail: `soft-404: {url} returns HTTP 200 for a route that should not exist`
- fail: `the product deep link itself returns HTTP {status}`
- fail: `the deep link returns HTTP {status} but carries only {n} visible characters before JavaScript runs (floor 2000): the page is a client-rendered shell`
- pass: `deep link HTTP {s}; invalid route correctly HTTP {s}; {n} visible characters present before JS`
Parameters: min_pre_js_visible_chars 2000, chosen by this project
Is it the recognized way to measure the behavior: Requesting a route known not to exist and reading the status is the standard soft-404 probe (it is what Search Console reports). Counting visible characters before JavaScript has no published method or threshold.

BRANCHES (each verdict branch of the rule; the behavior it rewards or penalizes; its source):
- fail_soft_404 (fail): HTTP 200 for a route that does not exist Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt (§15.5.5); https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes (soft 404).
- fail_deep_link_error (fail): the product's own deep link is not served Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt (§15 status codes).
- fail_client_rendered_shell (fail): penalizes a tool whose content arrives by JavaScript; the cited crawler documentation supports that model Source: none.
- pass_all_three (pass): real 404, served deep link, and at least 2000 visible characters before JavaScript; the last condition has no source Source: none.

CLAIMS:
A pass claims: The tool's deep link was served with at least 2000 characters of text before any script ran, and a made-up route under the tool returned a non-200 status.
A fail claims: Either a made-up route under the tool returned HTTP 200 (a soft 404), the deep link itself returned an error, or the deep link's content arrives only by JavaScript. It is not a claim that the tool is unusable by a browser or by a crawler that renders JavaScript.
Neither claims: Nothing about the tool's API, its data, or what a rendering client sees.

CONFOUNDS:
- a tool built as a single-page application that renders correctly in a browser and in Googlebot. Distinguished: no: the shell branch fails it.
- a soft 404 served by a CDN or framework default rather than the agency's choice. Distinguished: no; it is still what a client receives.
response_text: {"q1": {"answer": "yes", "why": "The two requirements the text attributes to sources are backed by quoted passages: the 404 definition is the verbatim RFC 9110 §15.5.5 sentence, and 'a 200 whose content says the page is an error is a soft 404 which Google treats as an error' is supported by 'Search Console will show a soft 404 error'. The deep-link-served requirement is not attributed to any source in the text. The pre-JavaScript content requirement is said plainly to have no cited source and the 2000-character floor is marked 'chosen by this project', with the branches table repeating 'Source: none'. Two small assertions go beyond the quoted passages but are not stated as source requirements: the '(or 410)' alternative is not in the RFC quote, and 'the app-shell model it describes is supported' is not in the Google quote (which only says 200 pages are queued for rendering); both are used to loosen, not tighten, what is demanded."}, "q2": {"answer": "yes", "why": "Two misreadings stay open. First, the fail claim says 'the deep link's content arrives only by JavaScript', but the test only establishes that fewer than 2000 visible characters were present before scripts ran; a server-rendered page with a short real text body (say 1200 characters plus a data table built by script) would fail and a reader would take the published claim as proof the page is an empty client-rendered shell, which was not measured. The claims disclaim usability by browsers and rendering crawlers but do not disclaim this. Second, the question frames the check as whether the tool answers 'honestly', and the confounds admit a CDN or framework default soft 404 is not distinguished; the claims do not say a fail is not a claim about the agency's own configuration choice, so a reader who knows the agency could read a soft-404 fail as agency-side misconfiguration or deception rather than an edge-platform default."}, "q3": {"answer": "yes", "terms": ["error-shell tokens", "visible characters (before JavaScript)", "app-shell model"], "why": "'Error-shell tokens' names what the harness reads in the invalid route's body but the entry never says which strings count or how they bear on the decision rule, which uses only the status. 'Visible characters before JavaScript' is the quantity the 2000 floor is applied to, yet the entry does not say how visibility is decided without a renderer (text nodes only, excluding script/style/nav, whitespace handling), and the entry itself concedes there is no published method. 'App-shell model' is used as the basis for saying the client-rendered pattern is supported, but is neither defined nor quoted. Soft 404, deep link, SI client, harness and the other project terms are defined in the entry or the project glossary."}}
